title: Hedge funds claiming diversification suffered collective losses in October from concentrated AI bets
dek: Hedge funds across nearly all mainstream strategies lost money simultaneously in October, showing that most gains over the past year were actually from implicit long AI exposure, not genuine diversified strategy returns.
why: To understand how last month's "perfect storm" happened and which funds truly decoupled (like Citadel), this episode provides specific position and risk control figures.
who: Institutional investors tracking hedge fund allocation, analysts researching multi-strategy funds, and founders and investors wanting to understand the AI bubble transmission chain.
skip: The final section about oil and crude crack spreads has little connection to the main AI thread and can be skipped.

points.h: Flagship funds claiming stability lost money collectively in October
points.body: Millennium, Point72, and Exodus Point—the funds with the most concentrated talent and assets, viewed by investors as most steadfast during crises—all lost money in October. Millennium, with ~14% annualized returns, fell 2.3% in a single month. By hedge fund logic, this is dereliction: investors buy hedge funds not to beat bull markets but to expect protection during downturns. In October, that protection failed entirely. The real shock is not the loss itself but the failure to hedge.

points.h: Funds claiming diversification were concentrated in the same few AI stocks
points.body: Vara, a fund with positions highly overlapping with certain AI narratives, crashed 33% in October yet remains positive year-to-date—showing how much that prior AI exposure returned. Whale Rock similarly fell 12%. These single-strategy funds' exposure is explicit: nearly all positions bet on the same small handful of AI stocks. When momentum reverses, no hedge can cushion the blow.

points.h: Data shows multi-strategy funds were herding into the same stocks
points.body: Pivotal Path's research shows the top 10 multi-strategy funds control ~$2.2 trillion in positions including leverage, yet the actual capital supporting those positions is only $300-350 billion—indicating extreme system leverage. This does not mean they were momentum trading; likely these firms independently judged but converged on the same liquid stocks that fit their risk frameworks. The danger lies in what happens when they all change their minds at once: forced selling cascades in sync, exactly as occurred in October.

points.h: Multi-strategy funds show no mercy to losing traders
points.body: Nishant explained the brutal internal risk controls of multi-strategy funds: a PM managing $100 loses 5% (=$5) and their allocation gets cut in half; if they continue to 7.5% total loss, they are force-liquidated and fired on the spot. This discipline is the core pitch of the multi-strategy model—prevent any one team's losses from dragging down the whole platform. But when all strategies turned bad at once in October, this very mechanism meant massive positions were cut simultaneously, actually accelerating the decline.

points.h: Money rushed to buy shares but top platforms closed to new capital
points.body: Millennium aimed to raise $20 billion this year, received over $30 billion in demand, ultimately took $22 billion. Meanwhile, D.E. Shaw, Point72, and Citadel combined returned $35-40 billion to investors. A paradox emerges: investors desperately want multi-strategy fund slots, yet the top platforms are capping size and returning capital. The reason: once you add enough teams, new positions no longer add real diversification—they just dilute the same underlying risk.

points.h: Thursday's crash was not emotion but mechanical chain reaction
points.body: Michael Ball attributes Thursday's crash to options market mechanics: when investors buy puts for downside protection, put sellers (market makers) must continuously sell to hedge their delta risk as prices fall, which itself depresses prices in a self-reinforcing spiral. Layer on leveraged ETFs, systematic vol-control strategies, and CTA trend-following funds all forced to cut positions on the same day—four mechanisms in sync—and you breach the S&P level that held for months.

points.h: New cloud operators halved in value, rate sensitivity is the weakness
points.body: Take Iron: a cloud stock once pitched as "Bitcoin miners transitioning to AI compute." Its price was $77 in November 2025, down to $21 at recording—roughly a 70% fall. These companies borrowed heavily to build data centers and are highly sensitive to interest rates and customer prepayment quality. Ball thinks the selloff is excessive because backlog orders and compute demand remain robust. But whether 2028 new projects get regulatory blocked remains genuinely unresolved.

points.h: Huang's governance turmoil failed to ripple through the market
points.body: Markets might have feared that Nvidia governance trouble would transmit through the AI chain. But Ball observed the actual impact was limited: Nvidia itself declined modestly and AI/semiconductor stocks rebounded days later. His reading: AI is now too large for Nvidia or Anthropic alone to move the needle. One company's governance headline cannot shake the whole narrative anymore. Stock moves now track mechanical forces like short covering more than fundamental narrative shifts.
